disease_info: Delusional Disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more persistent, non-bizarre or less clearly bizarre delusions lasting at least one month, in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thinking, or marked mood episodes that would suggest schizophrenia or a mood disorder with psychotic features. Outside of the delusional beliefs, overall functioning is often relatively preserved, and behavior may appear largely appropriate, which can delay recognition and treatment. The content of the delusions is typically systematized and circumscribed (e.g., persecutory, jealous, somatic, grandiose, or erotomanic themes), and individuals may seek legal, medical, or interpersonal “solutions” to issues stemming from the fixed beliefs. The course is usually chronic, with limited insight and resistance to contradictory evidence, and it is differentiated from obsessive-compulsive or overvalued ideas by the degree of conviction and imperviousness to reasoning.

narrative.personality: Justin is a visionary yet somewhat disorganized IT leader who combines technical curiosity, artistic sensibility, and a generally relaxed, mentoring style with a tendency to get absorbed in his interests.
narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Justin’s company underwent a major restructuring that placed him under a new, more controlling executive who questioned several of his long-standing infrastructure decisions and hinted that his team might be outsourced. For someone who had built his identity around being a trusted, forward-thinking IT architect and mentor, this felt like a deep professional invalidation, especially as budget cuts delayed projects he believed were essential and sidelined him from strategic meetings. He began to ruminate extensively, alone in his office and on long hikes, poring over system logs, emails, and casual remarks from colleagues in an effort to make sense of what he saw as a pattern of targeted undermining, gradually organizing these interpretations into a rigid explanatory framework that he shared only with his wife and a few close coworkers. Over the following 14 months, his insistence on this explanation increasingly strained relationships at work and at home, and when his wife noticed he was turning down community mentoring events and spending evenings gathering “evidence” instead of playing guitar or gardening, she encouraged him—along with HR’s suggestion after a tense meeting—to seek a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m here because I have these beliefs about what’s going on around me, and no matter what anyone says, I just can’t shake them.”

narrative.personality: Michelle is a chronically worried but imaginative and meticulous young woman who channels her energy into highly organized art-making and community-focused creative projects.
narrative.stressor: Michelle’s difficulties began in the months following a chaotic, short-lived marriage that ended in a contentious divorce, during which her ex-partner repeatedly accused her of being untrustworthy and unstable in front of friends and family. Coming from a background where she already felt academically insecure and socially underestimated, these attacks on her character were deeply humiliating and left her scanning every interaction at work and in the local art scene for signs that people were judging or talking about her. Over the next year, she spent more and more time journaling late into the night, re-reading text messages, and mentally replaying conversations at the register and at open-mic nights, gradually weaving together a tightly organized narrative about why others were behaving the way they were toward her, which she guarded fiercely despite reassurances from a few supportive peers. As her conviction hardened, conflicts with her manager and estrangement from some friends increased, and when a volunteer coordinator at an art fair gently suggested she talk to someone because her explanations for minor mishaps had become unusually intense and inflexible, Michelle reluctantly agreed to see a psychiatrist at the urging of her mother.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep holding on to these beliefs about what people are really doing and saying about me, and I can’t let them go even when everyone tells me I’m wrong.”

narrative.personality: Wanda is a calm, harmony-seeking young woman who enjoys predictable routines, caring for plants, and nurturing others through food and crafts, though she can be casually disorganized with practical details.
narrative.stressor: Wanda’s problems started after a minor but lingering health scare about two years ago, when she developed persistent stomach discomfort that multiple clinic visits and basic tests failed to clearly explain. Feeling brushed off by busy providers and worried about how any serious diagnosis could affect her ability to work outdoors and support her family, she began reading online forums and home-remedy blogs, relating the vague physical sensations she noticed during long days in the sun to increasingly specific ideas about what must be wrong. Over the following year, instead of easing with repeated reassurances, her conviction about the nature and cause of her condition gradually solidified, shaping how she talked about her body to coworkers and family, even as she continued to show up for her landscaping job and keep up with most of her hobbies. When a trusted aunt, concerned by how fixed and elaborate Wanda’s explanations had become despite normal medical evaluations, persuaded her primary care doctor to refer her for a mental health assessment, Wanda agreed to see a psychiatrist mainly to prove that her beliefs were justified.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I have these beliefs about what’s going on with my body, and I just can’t be convinced otherwise, no matter what the doctors tell me.”
